title: Effective classification of polynomially testable hereditary graph properties
formal: Does there exist a deterministic Turing machine that, on input a finite list \(\mathcal F\) of finite simple graphs, always halts and correctly decides whether \(\mathcal F\) has the polynomial sampling property below? The input is the finite list of forbidden induced patterns. No running-time bound is imposed on this classification algorithm. The constants in the sampling property may depend on the whole fixed list, but must hold simultaneously at every graph order and proximity parameter.
definitions: A finite simple graph is an undirected graph with no loops or multiple edges. Write \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), with \([0]=\varnothing\). A valid input list \(\mathcal F=(F_1,\ldots,F_r)\), \(r\ge0\), is encoded by the orders and full Boolean adjacency matrices of its members on \([|V(F_i)|]\); the matrices are symmetric with zero diagonal. Integer orders and list lengths are binary encoded with delimiters. Repeated graphs and the graph of order zero are allowed. For \(n\ge1\), let \(\mathcal P_{\mathcal F,n}\) consist of all graphs on \([n]\) with no induced copy of any \(F_i\). An induced copy of \(F_i\) is an injection \(\phi:V(F_i)\to[n]\) such that for every distinct \(u,v\), \(\{u,v\}\in E(F_i)\) if and only if \(\{\phi(u),\phi(v)\}\in E(G)\). For a graph \(G\) on \([n]\), define \[d_{\mathcal F}(G)=\frac{1}{n^2}\min_{H\in\mathcal P_{\mathcal F,n}}|E(G)\mathbin{\triangle}E(H)|\] when the set is nonempty, and \(d_{\mathcal F}(G)=+\infty\) otherwise. Symmetric difference counts each added or deleted undirected edge once. A graph is \(\varepsilon\)-far if \(d_{\mathcal F}(G)>\varepsilon\), with strict inequality. For an integer \(s\ge1\), the canonical sampling test chooses a uniformly random subset \(S\subseteq[n]\) of size \(\min\{n,s\}\), queries all \(\binom{|S|}{2}\) adjacency bits within it, and rejects exactly when \(G[S]\) contains an induced member of \(\mathcal F\). Local sampling and finite pattern checking are not charged as adjacency queries. The polynomial sampling property means that there exist integers \(C,a\ge1\) such that for every rational \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\), every \(n\ge1\), and every \(\varepsilon\)-far graph \(G\), this test with \(s=\lceil C\varepsilon^{-a}\rceil\) rejects with probability at least \(2/3\). Probability is solely over the uniform subset. For every member of \(\mathcal P_{\mathcal F,n}\), the test accepts with probability one. There is no extra promise on the host graph. The empty forbidden list defines all graphs; if the list contains the order-zero graph, every test rejects since the empty induced copy exists in every sample. These conventions also specify empty property classes at individual orders. The classifier takes only \(\mathcal F\), not \(n,\varepsilon,C\) or \(a\), and need not output the constants. It is one finite program with no advice or oracle, required to output YES exactly for lists with the sampling property and NO for all other valid lists. It may reject malformed encodings; it must halt on every input string.
answer_criterion: Provide a complete Lean-checked proof that such a total classifier exists, or a complete Lean-checked proof that no such classifier exists. The affirmative answer must establish termination and both directions of correctness on every finite forbidden list. The negative answer must rule out every deterministic Turing program as a total correct classifier. An equivalent condition that still quantifies over unbounded host graphs and all accuracy parameters is not by itself a decision algorithm. Proving polynomial testability for one family or a finite collection of families does not meet the universal classification target.
why: Asks whether the efficient sampling regime of hereditary graph testing can be recognized from a finite description, turning a broad classification programme into a precise decidability target.

importance.reason: An effective formulation of the major finite-family classification problem; it separates polynomial sampling from mere testability and abstract quantitative equivalences.

progress.text: Alon–Shapira establish general one-sided hereditary graph testability; the guarantee is qualitative and does not give polynomial sample bounds for every family.
Alon–Fox prove polynomial testability of cographs, or induced-four-vertex-path freeness. Their path notation counts edges.
Gishboliner–Shapira establish the checked finite-family sufficient and necessary conditions, including examples showing that they do not coincide.
The checked author revision and Combinatorica publication give a single-exponential induced-four-cycle bound and state the polynomial conjecture separately.
The survey states the finite-family structural classification as Problem 3.14, with the four-cycle as the first key open case.
The ECCC container characterization provides explicit tester/container parameter conversions. No total classifier from an arbitrary finite forbidden list is established in its inspected main results.

status_note: Uncertain for the explicitly retained effective decidability target. On 15 September 2026, the finite-family theorem and counterexamples, the 2025 structural classification problem, the later induced-four-cycle manuscript and the August 2026 ECCC container characterization were checked. The source asks a structural characterization; that does not itself certify openness of the additional decision-procedure requirement. The checked quantitative theorem does not provide such a classifier, and a bounded later-work search did not verify a resolution. Source proofs were not independently verified or formalized in Lean.

context_blocks.text: Each finite forbidden list defines an elementary graph-membership test: search the input graph for the listed induced patterns. The classification problem has a different input and quantifier structure. Given the list alone, it asks whether every sufficiently distant host graph has a small random sample witnessing a violation, with a single polynomial bound across all host orders and accuracy parameters.

The inherited card added an effectiveness requirement to the source’s structural characterization programme. This review preserves that choice and makes its machine model explicit. The source does not itself assert the decidability statement or its negation, so the current scientific status of this effective target is recorded as uncertain.

Hereditary properties are closed under taking induced subgraphs, and every forbidden-induced-pattern property here is hereditary. General hereditary testing gives some size-independent sample bound. It does not guarantee polynomial dependence on reciprocal distance, which is the distinction the classifier must recognize.

The finite list remains fixed during each sampling problem. Reading every pair in a sample squares the sample size, so polynomial vertex sampling and the resulting polynomial adjacency-query bound agree at this level of precision. The classifier itself is allowed arbitrary finite time; it is not a polynomial-time recognition question.

For nonempty finite families in the usual nontrivial setting, the checked sufficient condition is that the family contain a bipartite graph, a co-bipartite graph and a split graph. Bipartite means a partition into two independent sets; co-bipartite means a partition into two cliques, with arbitrary edges between them; split means a partition into a clique and an independent set. One graph may fill several roles. A necessary condition requires bipartite and co-bipartite members.

The necessary and sufficient conditions do not coincide. The paper provides families meeting the former that are hard to test, and the split-graph property supplies a positive case outside the latter. For split graphs the forbidden list consists of the four-cycle, its complement and the five-cycle; none is itself split. These examples prevent turning either condition into a complete classification.

Even among single forbidden patterns, the induced four-cycle and its complement are the outstanding polynomial-testability cases identified by the survey. The four-vertex path case, whose free graphs are cographs, has a polynomial tester.

The checked induced-four-cycle theorem gives single-exponential reciprocal-distance dependence. It is relevant progress on a member of the class being classified, but does not establish the polynomial sampling property for that member.

The August 2026 container characterization supplies explicit quantitative translations between tester bounds and combinatorial container parameters. Its premises still range over all large host graphs and accuracy parameters. The inspected statements do not give a procedure that halts on each finite forbidden list and decides whether polynomial parameters exist.

An effective positive classification would turn a finite pattern description into a reliable recognition method for the polynomial testing regime. An undecidability result would instead limit such systematic recognition, even though checking any particular finite host graph against the list is straightforward.

sentences: A finite family of forbidden induced graphs specifies a hereditary graph property.
The question asks whether a total algorithm can decide from that family whether its canonical one-sided test has polynomial reciprocal-distance sample complexity.
Every query is an adjacency check, while rejection must exhibit a forbidden pattern with both its edges and its nonedges.
Known structural conditions and quantitative container equivalences do not give the total finite-input classifier required by this card.
Algorithmic decidability is the inherited editorial specification, and its status is uncertain rather than attributed verbatim as a conjecture of the structural survey.
